metadata.title: Design and simulation of sour water unit: A case study of port Harcourt refining company
metadata.description: The simulation of a 35.0m3/hr sour water plant model using aspen hysys process simulator was carried out using 3 different fluids; steam, kerosene and naphtha, respectively.  The major equipment in the plant model are: 3-phase separator, heat exchanger and absorber tower.  The results of the parameter obtained from aspen HYSYS were presented in terms of material balance, Energy balance, sizing and costing.  The material balance result in terms of composition (mole fraction) obtained from the absorber outlet stream for treated water were constant for naphtha and kerosene plants showing 0.0248, 0.0004, 0.9748 and 0.0000 for NH3, H2S, H2O and oil, respectively while that of steam plant gave 0.0296, 0.0004, 0.9699 and 0.0000 for NH3, H2S, H2O and oil, respectively. The result in terms of material balance shows total elimination of oil from sour water with 97.48% recovery of water, 0.04% reduced rate of H2S and 2.48% reduced rate of NH3. The energy requirement of each plant model in terms of heat duty (kJ/hr) for heater and heat exchanger for steam, kerosene and naphtha plant models were also examined. Steam plant heat duty for heater and heat exchangers gave: 6.798 x 106 KJ/hr and 8.031 x 106 KJ/hr, respectively, kerosene plant heat duty for heater and heat exchanger were 8.031 x 106 KJ/hr and 2.067 x 107 KJ/hr, respectively, naphtha plant heat duty for heater and heat exchanger were 8.031 x 106 KJ/hr and 1.238 x 107 KJ/hr, respectively. Sizing results of major equipment such as 3-phase separator, heat exchanger and absorber column for steam, kerosene and naphtha plant were obtained from aspen HYSYS simulation along with cost analysis.

metadata.title: Comparative study of CO2-N2 and N2-N2 dual expansion in natural gas liquefaction process
metadata.description: The processes were modelled using the Aspen Hysys version 11. The paper compared two refrigeration systems with different refrigerants, CO2-N2 and N2-N2, and their expenders. The parameters compared are the liquefaction power, specific power, production capacity, and heat duty of the expander cycle. The liquefaction power of CO2-N2 (547.669kW) is lower than that of N2-N2 (815.85kW). The specific power consumption for CO2-N2 was 0.44096kW/kg, and for N2-N2 was 0.6569kW/kg. The production capacity N2-N2 gave a higher value of 6945.6MTPA than CO2-N2 4904.38MTPA.

metadata.description: Ushbu maqolada suyuq uglevodlar asosidagi yoqilg‘i sarfi fraksiyalarini bug‘latish jarayonini samarali va barqaror boshqarish masalalari tadqiq etiladi. Bug‘latish jarayoni neft va neft mahsulotlarini qayta ishlashda muhim texnologik bosqichlardan biri bo‘lib, mahsulot sifati, energiya tejamkorligi hamda ishlab chiqarish xavfsizligini ta’minlashda hal qiluvchi ahamiyatga ega. Tadqiqot doirasida an’anaviy boshqaruv usullarining kamchiliklari tahlil qilinib, zamonaviy texnik vositalar, jumladan, raqamli sensorlar, avtomatlashtirilgan boshqaruv tizimlari, real vaqt monitoringi hamda sun’iy intellektga asoslangan optimallashtirish algoritmlarini joriy etish imkoniyatlari yoritilgan. Shuningdek, bug‘latish jarayonining termodinamik modellari va simulyatsion platformalar yordamida boshqaruv parametrlarini optimallashtirish masalalari ko‘rib chiqilgan. O‘tkazilgan tahlillar zamonaviy boshqaruv texnologiyalarini qo‘llash energiya sarfini kamaytirish, fraksiyalar sifatini barqarorlashtirish va ishlab chiqarish samaradorligini oshirishga xizmat qilishini ko‘rsatadi.

metadata.title: Production of Synthetic Fuels From High Density Polyethylene (HDPE) Waste Through Pyrolysis: Experimental And Simulation Approaches
metadata.description: Production of synthetic fuels through the pyrolysis of high density polyethylene (HDPE) waste was examined. A semibatch reactor was designed and fabricated to pyrolyse HDPE waste in the absence of catalyst at a residence time of 60 minutes and final temperature of 425oC. At the end of the process, 51.84%, 45.33%, and 2.83%, liquid product, char and evolved gaseous product were obtained respectively. The temperature progression for the process was examined. The pyrolysis oil obtained was light brown in colour, highly flammable, with a density of 772.6 kg/m3 and pH of 5.5. ASPEN Hysys was used to simulate the pyrolysis process. Simulation results revealed an oil yield of 97%, a gas yield of about 2% and a <1% char yield. The simulation revealed the commencement of reaction at about 325oC with an optimum reaction temperature of 450oC. If properly optimized HDPE is revealed to be an excellent feedstock of pyrolysis.

metadata.title: Enhancing Reformate Yield on Naphtha Reforming Unit by Upgrading Secondary-Recovery Schemes
metadata.description:
ABSTRACT

In the oil processing industry (refinery), the process of upgrading octane number of naphtha fraction is carried out at Naphtha Reforming Unit (NRU). Some NRU scan produce high purity hydrogen gas. The high purity of hydrogen gas products correlates with the increase in yield of reformate and LPG in the NRU. Previous studies have increased the reformate yield by optimizing the reactor system, while this research is optimizing the secondary recovery system which also has an impact on reformate yield. For this purpose, a single stage contact recovery system is used in the secondary recovery system of the NRU with the addition of several other equipment. The results show that lowering the contact temperature can increase the reformate yield and product purity of hydrogen gas. From the economic analysis shows that by upgrading the basic scheme to a low temperature scheme, there must be an additional CAPEX (capital expenditure) of 4.91 M USD, and OPEX (operating expenses) of 2.26 M USD annually. Considering the 7.89 billion USD income from the additional reformate product, the investment payout period (POT) will be one year and is considered feasible.

metadata.description: The simulation of a 35.0m3/hr sour water plant model using aspen hysys process simulator was carried out using 3 different fluids; steam, kerosene and naphtha, respectively.  The major equipment in the plant model are: 3-phase separator, heat exchanger and absorber tower.  The results of the parameter obtained from aspen HYSYS were presented in terms of material balance, Energy balance, sizing and costing.  The material balance result in terms of composition (mole fraction) obtained from the absorber outlet stream for treated water were constant for naphtha and kerosene plants showing 0.0248, 0.0004, 0.9748 and 0.0000 for NH3, H2S, H2O and oil, respectively while that of steam plant gave 0.0296, 0.0004, 0.9699 and 0.0000 for NH3, H2S, H2O and oil, respectively. The result in terms of material balance shows total elimination of oil from sour water with 97.48% recovery of water, 0.04% reduced rate of H2S and 2.48% reduced rate of NH3. The energy requirement of each plant model in terms of heat duty (kJ/hr) for heater and heat exchanger for steam, kerosene and naphtha plant models were also examined. Steam plant heat duty for heater and heat exchangers gave: 6.798 x 106 KJ/hr and 8.031 x 106 KJ/hr, respectively, kerosene plant heat duty for heater and heat exchanger were 8.031 x 106 KJ/hr and 2.067 x 107 KJ/hr, respectively, naphtha plant heat duty for heater and heat exchanger were 8.031 x 106 KJ/hr and 1.238 x 107 KJ/hr, respectively. Sizing results of major equipment such as 3-phase separator, heat exchanger and absorber column for steam, kerosene and naphtha plant were obtained from aspen HYSYS simulation along with cost analysis.

metadata.title: Production of Synthetic Fuels From High Density Polyethylene (HDPE) Waste Through Pyrolysis: Experimental And Simulation Approaches
metadata.description: Production of synthetic fuels through the pyrolysis of high density polyethylene (HDPE) waste was examined. A semibatch reactor was designed and fabricated to pyrolyse HDPE waste in the absence of catalyst at a residence time of 60 minutes and final temperature of 425oC. At the end of the process, 51.84%, 45.33%, and 2.83%, liquid product, char and evolved gaseous product were obtained respectively. The temperature progression for the process was examined. The pyrolysis oil obtained was light brown in colour, highly flammable, with a density of 772.6 kg/m3 and pH of 5.5. ASPEN Hysys was used to simulate the pyrolysis process. Simulation results revealed an oil yield of 97%, a gas yield of about 2% and a <1% char yield. The simulation revealed the commencement of reaction at about 325oC with an optimum reaction temperature of 450oC. If properly optimized HDPE is revealed to be an excellent feedstock of pyrolysis.

metadata.title: Enhancing Reformate Yield on Naphtha Reforming Unit by Upgrading Secondary-Recovery Schemes
metadata.description:
ABSTRACT

In the oil processing industry (refinery), the process of upgrading octane number of naphtha fraction is carried out at Naphtha Reforming Unit (NRU). Some NRU scan produce high purity hydrogen gas. The high purity of hydrogen gas products correlates with the increase in yield of reformate and LPG in the NRU. Previous studies have increased the reformate yield by optimizing the reactor system, while this research is optimizing the secondary recovery system which also has an impact on reformate yield. For this purpose, a single stage contact recovery system is used in the secondary recovery system of the NRU with the addition of several other equipment. The results show that lowering the contact temperature can increase the reformate yield and product purity of hydrogen gas. From the economic analysis shows that by upgrading the basic scheme to a low temperature scheme, there must be an additional CAPEX (capital expenditure) of 4.91 M USD, and OPEX (operating expenses) of 2.26 M USD annually. Considering the 7.89 billion USD income from the additional reformate product, the investment payout period (POT) will be one year and is considered feasible.

metadata.title: Physicochemical Characteristics, Process Optimization, and Energy Efficiency of Hydrogen Production from Methanol, Ethanol, and Glycerol: A Comparative Review
metadata.description: Hydrogen production has indeed been one of the hottest topics these days in the connection toward sustainable energy. Hydrogen has potentially huge applications as a clean and flexible energy carrier to power nearly all applications where fossil fuels are used-fuel cells through the ladder of industrial processes. A number of methods have been developed to produce hydrogen, but one of the most promising strategies uses renewable feedstocks, such as ethanol, methanol, and glycerol. This article provides an exhaustive survey and comparison of three emerging technologies for hydrogen production from these feedstocks based on their physicochemical properties, technological feasibility, and economic viability. It deeply explores the inner conversion mechanisms and chemical reactions involved in the process, discussing the determining factors that influence the efficiency, environmental effect, and scale-up viability of each one. Thus, conversion process evaluation for ethanol, methanol, and glycerol is undertaken under different operational conditions defined as temperature, pressure, and catalyst type. All these parameters have critical control over the hydrogen yield and purity produced and the generation of byproducts including carbon dioxide and water. To assure the evaluation's robustness and dependability, simulations of these processes were done using a state-of-the-art modeling suite, that is, Aspen Plus and Aspen Hysys software. These enable very accurate quantification of thermodynamic and kinetic evaluations for each method by giving insights into their energy and material flows at different moments in the production process. The simulations also help in optimizing the operating conditions to achieve maximum hydrogen yield while.

metadata.title: Dataset for publication "Onboard carbon capture for circular marine fuels"
metadata.description:
Dataset associated with the publication "Onboard carbon capture for circular marine fuels" by Margarita A. Charalambous, Valentin Negri, Valentin Kamm, and Gonzalo Guillén-Gosálbez, published in the journal ACS Sustainable Chemistry and Engineering. Link to publication

The dataset includes all the codes, environmental databases, simulations, figures, and economic data. The codes and the excel data are required to reproduce the plots embedded in the main manuscript.

The dataset includes 3 Excel files. The content of each dataset is here elucidated:

Data.xlsx: Inventory datasets used for the economic assessment. Includes the costs per tonne kilometer (tkm) for methanol and natural gas ships, and also the final data, including the sensitivity analysis used for plotting.  
Circular-marine-fuels-2030.xlsx: life cycle inventories used for 2030. Includes the production of CO2, H2, methanol, natural gas, and the transport inventories for the three ships (methanol, natural gas, BAU). This is an excel file database that can be directly used in Brightway, using Activity browser. The database was created using data from premise compatible with Ecoinvent v3.10. 
Circular-marine-fuels-2050.xlsx: life cycle inventories used for 2050. Includes the production of CO2, H2, methanol, natural gas, and the transport inventories for the three ships (methanol, natural gas, BAU). This is an excel file database that can be directly used in Brightway, using Activity browser. The database was created using data from premise compatible with Ecoinvent v3.10. 

The dataset includes 2 python jupyter notebooks. The content of each dataset is here elucidated:

env_calc.ipynb: Python code that shows how the calculation of the life cycle impact assessment is performed and how the results are plotted.
Plotting.ipynb: Python code that shows how to plot the economic results. 

The dataset includes 4 process simulations. The content of each simulationis here elucidated:

MeOH_Production.hsc: Aspen HYSYS file that includes the process simulation of methanol production, using CO2 from ships and DAC. 
Capture_onboard_methanol.hsc: Aspen HYSYS file that includes the process simulation of capture onboard methanol ship. 
Capture_onboard_NG.hsc: Aspen HYSYS file that includes the process simulation of capture onboard natural gas ship. 
LNG_Production.apw: Aspen PLUS file that includes the process simulation for natural gas production.
